newsitem.title: UK: UK book stores compete for sales over the Internet.
newsitem.headline: UK book stores compete for sales over the Internet.

text.p: Two of Britain's leading booksellers said on Monday they would launch Internet bookstores, jumping on the growing bandwagon of bookchains seeking wider sales via the Web.
Dillons, owned by EMI Group Plc, said its Internet site, called The Book Pl@ce (http://www.thebookplace.com), will be launched on September 12.

Blackwells, which has been selling a limited number of books on the Internet since 1995, said it had invested a seven-figure sum to relaunch its site (http://www.blackwell.co.uk/bookshops) with a new look and a choice of 1.5 million titles in October.

The Book Pl@ce, which cost one million pounds ($1.6 million) to set up and has taken two years to prepare, will have 1.2 million titles on sale. Dillons expects up to 2,000 orders a month and 100,000 visitors in the first six months, a company spokesman said.
Herbert Kim, head of Internet marketing and sales for Blackwells, said Internet bookstores were a booming market.
Although many commercial sites on the Internet's World Wide Web have yet to attract significant volume, bookstores have been among the most successful sites.

U.S.-based Amazon.com Inc (http://www.amazon.com) has been setting the pace for book sales on the Internet since its founding in Seattle two years ago. The company, which sells books only via the Internet and has not even a warehouse to call its own, posted sales of $27.9 million in the 1997 second quarter. But it has yet to turn a profit.
Barnes & Noble, a New York-based book retailer with more than 1,000 stores and $2.45 billion in sales in 1996, launched its own Internet bookstore (http://www.barnesandnoble.com) last May.

British bookchain Waterstone's, owned by WH Smith Group Plc and a high-street rival to Dillons and Blackwell, launched a virtual bookshop (http://www.waterstone's.co.uk) last October and has on average 80,000 visitors a month to its Web site.

Blackwell's Kim said the chain has aggressive goals for its Internet site. "Our sales target is to hit 1.5 million pounds by the end of the next fiscal year and then 10 million pounds the year after that," he told Reuters in a phone interview.

"They are aggressive targets, but we're in a business that has done essentially nothing yet," Kim said. "It only accounts for 0.01 percent of retail sales, but it has grown 50 percent in the last year."
Bookstores are attracted to selling via the Internet because it allows them to offer more titles for less money, said Sally Taplin, new media manager at Waterstone's.

"In high street stores the maximum stock capacity is 150,000 titles because retail space is so expensive," Taplin said. "Internet book stores can offer a massive amount of titles without having to store them in one place."
Blackwells believes its Internet book store will appeal to the public because it makes browsing easy.

"There are so many books out there and so many titles, that it's difficult to find the one you want unless you know the title and author," Kim said. "People can search our Internet store and get results with only fragments of information."
Blackwell's expects a high proportion of its Internet sales to come from countries like Sweden, Japan and Brazil, where the retail market for English language books is more expensive, he added.
